articles.title_orig: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.title_zh: Poised for breakout moment in Latin America, Pope Leo also faces test of health
articles.content_orig:
Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted.
But Leo XIV is forging ahead with a grueling 12-day visit, which includes Uruguay, Argentina, and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades.
He plans to cover a lot of ground – around 19,000 miles – while in Latin America. From November 6 to 17, the pope is scheduled to take 14 flights (including two in a helicopter), give 36 speeches and participate in around 50 events in what is one of the most intense papal trips of recent years.
He will also visit Cusco, Peru, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea-level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath. During the whole trip, he’ll travel to 10 cities, preside at large open-air Masses and vigils and meet with political leaders.
The trip, especially Cusco’s altitude, has raised questions about his health and the precautions being taken while there. It has also shone a light on a region that has profoundly shaped him and set his path to the papacy.
The pontiff had surgery last month to remove a third of his right lung after a small growth was discovered during routine checks, which was later confirmed as cancer. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said afterward that there were “no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place,” and doctors have said he does not need further treatment.
Vatican officials told reporters that Pope Leo will have a medical team available to him for the trip but stressed that no special measures are being taken. “We’re speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health,” the Vatican spokesman said ahead of the visit.
He explained the pope will travel with the “ordinary medical assistance,” including doctors, nurses and an ambulance, which usually travels with the pope’s convoy. But the spokesman said he wasn’t going into too much detail as the pope does not have a “permanent condition.” And if the Vatican medical team needs any help, one of the journalists traveling with the pope is also a doctor.
Montse Alvarado, the new head of Vatican Communications, told journalists on Tuesday that the pope’s “stamina is fantastic,” and that “he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen.”
Dr. Matthew Triplette, a pulmonologist from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, told CNN the risk of a medical emergency during the trip is “low” but that this could include “either a collapsed lung or blood clots.”
Triplette said the pope may be advised to “take low-dose blood thinners or use exercises or compression devices” to lower the possibility of blood clots in his legs when flying, which could cause major issues if they spread to the lungs. He added that the pope may feel more fatigue with exertion, particularly because there is less oxygen available at altitude.
In the aftermath of his surgery, many speculated that the trip would be canceled.
“I must confess that, until just a few days ago, I was among the few who had serious doubts about whether this trip could even take place,” Guzmán Carriquiry, a Uruguayan former Vatican official who worked on Latin American issues for nearly 50 years in the church’s central administration, told reporters on Tuesday.
But he also pointed out that the pope’s health team gave him the green light. “This suggests that his doctors believe the pope possesses a robust physical constitution; it also serves as a testament to the pope’s ardent desire and determination to go out and meet our people,” he said.
But Carriquiry noted that he would have removed Cusco from the agenda if he had organized the trip.
While Leo XIV is known for his gentle, low-key style, he is determined.
Answering a question from CNN, Alvarado said the pope “personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” and that he was looking forward to returning to Latin America.
The continent, and Peru in particular, is close to his heart, and Alvarado said the pope would speak off the cuff frequently in Spanish, a language he is fluent in.
“He’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go,” is how Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican foreign minister, put it at an event in Rome at the end of last month.
The Peruvian part of the trip will be emotional, as Leo arrives there “as an adopted brother, adopted by the Peruvian people,” said Carriquiry.
The pope, who remains a Peruvian citizen, had three stints in Peru, having first arrived there in his 30s. He also served as Bishop of Chiclayo in the northwest part of the country from 2015 to 2023.
The pope will return to Chiclayo during the trip and is expected to receive a rapturous welcome. Leo is remembered fondly in the city, where he was considered a hands-on bishop who was known to travel across his diocese on horseback.
“The pope spent many years living amongst the simple, poor and devout people of rural Latin America in northern Peru, as a missionary and a pastor,” Carriquiry, who is the former secretary of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, said.
Leo is expected to draw huge crowds when he’s there, with estimates of around 1.2 million people expected to attend his final Mass of the trip at Las Palmas Airbase in Lima.
He is also expected to draw huge crowds in Argentina, where more than a million people are expected to attend his Mass in Buenos Aires.
The late Pope Francis, the first Argentine pontiff, never made a visit to his home country, so Leo’s visit is one that is generating intense interest.
Francis never gave a clear reason as to why he didn’t visit Argentina. Carriquiry, a close friend of the late pope, said it “remains an enigma.”
Leo XIV’s visit will underline his plans to continue the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Argentine President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
Both Milei and Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori are notable figures in Latin America’s right-wing surge. They also enjoy support from the Trump administration, which Leo has publicly disagreed with — particularly on migration issues.
Leo XIV would not have been elected pope had he not been sent to Peru as a young Augustinian missionary.
His time in Latin America put him on a path to be spotted by Pope Francis. It was Francis who appointed the then-Rev. Robert Prevost as bishop in Chiclayo before later bringing him to Rome and naming him a cardinal.
All of this set him up as a candidate in the 2025 conclave. While Leo is the first pope from the United States and grew up in Chicago, his experience in Latin America has profoundly influenced his outlook.
In Peru, he served in the birthplace of liberation theology, a movement focused on social and political action to help the poor and oppressed. As a bishop, he was known for organizing practical assistance for those affected by floods or in need of medical equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic.
He served in a church in Peru which emphasized an inclusive model, giving greater roles to those not ordained as priests and bishops, including women.
Leo’s time in Peru also saw him exposed to the fallout of the clerical abuse crisis, including a major scandal involving a powerful Catholic group . The Vatican says the pope will have two meetings with abuse survivors during his trip, one in Argentina and another in Peru.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO Valuation Expectations Pressured After AI Rout
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Valuation Expectations Pressured After AI Rout
articles.content_orig:
Prospective buyers are discussing a $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion range, down from $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion, according to Bloomberg
Anthropic is facing lower valuation expectations for its initial public offering after a steep selloff in AI stocks, with prospective buyers discussing a range of $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, according to Bloomberg .
Formal marketing for the offering is due to begin next week, according to Bloomberg. Deliberations are still under way, and nothing final has been settled. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.
The Nasdaq $NDAQ 100 fell 6.4% on Thursday, a decline that erased $2.3 trillion of market capitalization and set a one-session record. Some investors had informed the deal's bankers that they considered roughly $1.4 trillion to $1.5 trillion a reasonable price, according to Bloomberg. Investors had put the figure at up to $2 trillion at the start of October.
Questions about the valuation grew louder when Democrats swept Congress, which raised the possibility of tougher oversight of data center buildouts, according to Bloomberg. The Cboe Volatility Index jumped Thursday to a peak not seen since April 2025.
Stephan Kemper, chief investment officer at BNP Paribas Wealth Management Germany, said the price tag could have to land at the bottom of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion range discussed earlier, or even 10% to 15% beneath it, according to Bloomberg.
Michael Alfaro, chief investment officer at hedge fund Gallo Partners, told Bloomberg ahead of Thursday's selloff that Anthropic should aim for a valuation of $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion "in order to build a quality book." Max Kettner, chief multi-asset strategist at HSBC Holdings, told Bloomberg Radio that pricing the company near $1 trillion might feel safer, since it would lessen the chance of sharp swings after shares start trading.
Anthropic and its selling shareholders could launch marketing cautiously, aiming low on both offering size and valuation, and then lift those targets if early investor reaction is encouraging, according to Bloomberg. Delaying the offering is another option. Companies are required to have their filings public for no fewer than 15 calendar days ahead of formal marketing, though some hold off for weeks or months.
Anthropic had targeted a listing before the Nov. 26 Thanksgiving holiday , with bankers potentially starting the roadshow during the week of Nov. 9. Prospective investors then valued the Claude maker at between $1.8 trillion and $2 trillion.
The company filed an amended Form S-1 on Monday showing $33.24 billion in revenue for January through Sept. 30 and a net loss of $104 billion for the period. Its most recent funding round valued it at $965 billion. Anthropic plans to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT."

articles.title_orig: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
articles.title_zh: Peru airport officials discover 3,000 tarantulas smuggled inside dirty socks
articles.content_orig:
Three suitcases’ worth of the spiders were on their way to Germany, where they could fetch an estimated €1.5m
More than 3,000 tarantulas were seized at an airport in Lima on their way to Germany, Peruvian authorities said.
The spiders were hidden inside dirty socks contained in three suitcases carried by two Germans and a Polish citizen, the National Forestry and Wildlife Service (SERFOR) told Agence France-Presse on Thursday.
They were spotted after agents noticed some unusual wriggling inside the luggage during a routine customs inspection at Jorge Chávez international airport. “We noticed that some of them were moving. There were small ones and large ones,” said Cora Suarez, a SERFOR wildlife control technician.
One tarantula can sell for about €500 ($560) in Europe, Suarez said, meaning the wildlife trafficking scheme would be potentially worth €1.5m for just one trip.
The hidden arachnids, which came from several regions of Peru, were found in varying stages of development, from eggs and hatchlings to adults, Suarez said.
The Europeans accused of smuggling the tarantulas were detained by police specialising in environmental crimes and will face criminal proceedings, SERFOR said.
Illegal wildlife trafficking is a highly lucrative criminal activity that generates around $20bn annually worldwide, according to Interpol.
Such trafficking is among the primary causes of the loss of biodiversity on the planet.

articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite rebounded on Friday as some investors bought the dip in chip stocks following a punishing sell-off that sent the index into correction territory.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq bounced by 1.1%. The S&P 500 rose 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained under pressure, down by 518 points, or 1%.
A strong October jobs report sent Treasury yields higher, which held back the gains in equities.
Worries of a potential slowdown in data center construction following big Democratic wins in the House and Senate and key state governorships hit U.S. markets hard on Thursday.
The heavy selling Thursday sent the three major stock averages to their worst one-day losses since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.5%, closing more than 10% below its most recent high and putting it in what Wall Street regards as a correction. The broad-market S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%.
All 11 sectors in the S&P 500 closed lower, but shares of companies tied to the AI build-out led the decline.
During Friday's session, shares of Micron Technology were up 9% following a 17% decline on Thursday. Nvidia was up 3% after a 9% rout the day before.
"The scale of the falls in some of the market's biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in U.S. equity markets," Stuart Clark, portfolio manager at Quilter, said by email.
"With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500."
The "Magnificent Seven" stocks shed $1 trillion in total market capitalization on Thursday alone.
Top Democrats have been calling to curb the data center buildout since the Democrats' big election win. Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa of Texas, a key data center hub in the country, said in a CNN interview Thursday evening, "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."
Investors reacted to the latest nonfarm payrolls report, which came in much better than expected at an increase of 165,000 in October. That was well above the 59,000 that economists polled by Dow Jones had anticipated. The unemployment rate also moved down to 4.1%. Economists had expected it to hold steady at 4.2%.
All three major averages are poised for losses on the week, even after Wednesday's big rally in the wake of the election. The Nasdaq is off by some 4.4% and the S&P 500 by almost 3% through Thursday. The 30-stock Dow is the outperformer, lower by just 0.5% week to date.
Looking at the history of Nasdaq corrections shows tech stocks often find their footing over the next three-to-six months, but trading can remain rocky in the near term.
SpaceX -backer Ron Baron told CNBC on Friday that Democrats shouldn't go after Elon Musk amid controversies about the role of Musk-operated satellites in the war between Russia and Ukraine. Congressional hearings about the matter have been floated in Washington.
"[Musk] hasn't done anything wrong. Why would there be a hearing?" Baron said on " Squawk Box ."
Baron made the case that Musk is a good builder and that his various commercial endeavors are supportive of the White House's domestic industrial policies.
"It would be a bad thing if we were in America reliant on Silicon only coming from Taiwan. [Musk] is probably the only person in this country who is able to build things at scale at attractive prices. Only one," Baron said.
The U.S. economy added 165,00 jobs in October , much more than expected, and the unemployment rate slipped slightly to 4.1%.
Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected an increase of just 59,000 jobs. The Bureau of Labor Statistics also revised higher its readings for the prior two months, with a combined 84,000 more jobs added than previously reported.

The U.S. economy isn't expected to have produced much job growth in October, with employers reluctant to hire workers but also not cutting staff amid a shrinking labor force and a growing problem of long-term unemployment.
Economists are looking for a meager nonfarm payrolls gain of 59,000, a slight uptick from the 29,000 jobs produced in September, according to the Dow Jones consensus. That result would continue a pattern of sparse growth.
But that's kind of OK: The forecast also is that the unemployment rate will hold at a very low 4.2% rate, the product of a climate where a stagnant labor force reduces the need for outsized job increases to keep the jobless level steady.
"Long-term, we're not going to need as many jobs added to the economy to have stable employment because we have fewer people who are available to work," said Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at jobs site ZipRecruiter. "An aging workforce is pushing a lot of people into retirement. We have had decades of low birth rates, meaning we don't have a lot of people who are coming in to replace those retiring workers. And immigration is now down pretty significantly, which is reducing some of that prime-age employment."
Read the full story here .
President Donald Trump on Friday said he 100% is in favor of the artificial intelligence build-out, and will work with any state that wants to help support the technology's growth.
"They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say "NO" to the riches they bring!" he said in a post on Truth Social .
The post comes after many Democrats won races in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday by campaigning against data centers , the key facilities that are in high demand to help support AI. Some of those Democrats, at both the national and state level, have called for data center moratoriums.
European stock markets remained deeply in the red on Friday, with the regional Stoxx 600 index last down 1.7%, heading for its worst session since March. Tech continued to be one of the most resilient sectors, down just 0.2%.
U.S. tech looked broadly set for a rebound, according to premarket indicators.
The five worst performers from the Nasdaq on Thursday were all higher in premarket on Friday, with SanDisk Corporation last seen up 9.6%, Astera Labs up 8.1%, Lumentum Holdings up 8.55%, Micron Technology up 8.2% and Western Digital up 6.6%.
Oil prices rebounded a touch on Friday, extending earlier gains, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections, alongside prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough.
International benchmark Brent crude futures were recently higher by 36 cents, or 0.39%, to $98.65 a barrel,  having jumped to almost $100 a barrel earlier in the session. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were ahead 43 cents or 0.48% to $90.98 a barrel.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index was 1.26% lower in early deals, following deep losses in Asia-Pacific markets on Friday and a sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday .
All sectors were in the red, though technology saw among the smallest impact, down 0.8%. Media stocks tumbled 2.4% as health-care fell 2.2%.
The sharp sell-off in AI-related names this week reflects an adjustment in growth expectations to a more sustainable level, according to William de Gale, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Blue Box Asset Management — but it does not change "insatiable" levels of demand.

articles.title_zh: Why Amazon and Other AI Data-Center Stocks Will Be Post-Midterm Winners
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the reporting threshold in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC on Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data center operators tumbled.

articles.title_orig: Global market rout deepens after midterms intensify AI fears
articles.title_zh: Global market rout deepens after midterms intensify AI fears
articles.content_orig:
HONG KONG — An intensifying rout of tech stocks hit global markets Friday, with a surge of red tickers spreading from Wall Street to Asia and Europe after the blue wave of the U.S. midterm elections fueled fears over AI development .
The steep losses in Asia — Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020 — came after a dramatic plunge in U.S. tech stocks following the success of anti-AI candidates, which deepened concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom.
Some $2.3 billion in market value was wiped off the tech-focused Nasdaq 100, which dropped 6.3% Thursday. Another $2.8 trillion was erased from the S&P 500’s market value as it fell 4.4% — the worst day for both indexes in 18 months, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets.
U.S. futures were mixed early Friday, but European shares also opened lower after the dramatic sell-off continued in Asia.
South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 index fell as much as 6%, entering bear-market territory.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.
The picture was little better in Europe. London’s FTSE 100 index fell by nearly 2%, while the French and German indexes, CAC40 and DAX, took similar hits.
“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News in emailed comments.
The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are “clearly highly linked to the global AI capex cycle and hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC chief market strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.
The plunge came after the stunning midterm results that will see a crop of anti-AI and data center opponent politicians take office, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, the largest data center market in the country.
The Democratic Congress could tighten scrutiny of the industry, including AI infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs, adding to worries investors have about the profitability of these investments.
The months leading up to the American elections had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that initial valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
Some of the Asian companies at the heart of the AI supply chain  surged to astonishing heights.
The Chinese market offered access to frontier AI companies that recently began going public — months earlier than their American counterparts like Anthropic, which is still preparing for its IPO.
Model maker Z.ai rose by 2,000% in June after debuting in January.
But corrections came swiftly, with Z.ai now down over 80% since its peak and on Friday shedding another 10%.
Lofty valuations of other Chinese companies have also cratered, with mainland China’s Star 50 index, which comprises the country’s semiconductor and AI leaders, now at half of its June peak with half a trillion in market value wiped out.
On Friday, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”
That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.
“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.

U.S. President Donald Trump reiterated his promise of a “big, beautiful agreement” on Ukraine after holding a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, on Thursday.
Dmitriev, who heads the U.S.-sanctioned Russian sovereign wealth fund, was attending a White House event hosted by First Lady Melania Trump where she delivered remarks about the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky that she helped negotiate. Although Russian and Ukrainian officials were present at the event, Trump told reporters Thursday evening he had only met Dmitriev.

“Everyone’s gonna be thrilled,” the U.S. president added.
On Friday, Trump’s son-in-law and diplomatic envoy Jared Kushner said the president had discussed with several European leaders the need for “a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace.” Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and is poised to hit Kyiv with another winter bombardment in the grueling conflict.
“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Kushner wrote on social media .
Kushner and Trump’s comments come ahead of U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi, which will involve Russian and Ukrainian officials on Nov. 10-11.

The move to clean electricity will form the focus of the climate summit, which begins next week in coal-obsessed Turkey. The outlook doesn’t look good
Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
H olding a climate conference under the presidency of one coal-obsessed country might be regarded as a misfortune for the planet – sharing it between two starts to look provocative. But at this year’s Cop31 UN climate summit in Antalya, coal exporter Australia and coal consumer Turkey will be trying to shift the focus away from dirty fossil fuels and towards clean electricity, with a target on the table to meet 35% of final energy demand from electricity by 2035.
Will they succeed? The geopolitical outlook for Cop31 is worse than for almost any recent “conference of the parties” under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). Conflicts in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza are destabilising global alliances, an unpredictable White House is sowing economic uncertainty and AI is threatening to unleash digitised chaos.
But with an El Niño weather system supercharged by fossil fuels already wreaking havoc and yet to peak, the climate is showing where the real potential for earthbound catastrophe lies. For the next fortnight, Down to Earth will bring you twice-weekly updates from the Cop31 negotiations plus, when the gavel finally comes down, a final assessment of what progress has been made – and where negotiations have fallen short in Antalya.
But first, this week’s most important reads.
‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets
The Amazon’s canary in the coalmine: what a tropical fish can tell us about climate upheaval
The next global pandemic could be brewing on a mink farm in Utah – and little is being done to stop it
That Cop31 is happening in Antalya, but presided over by Australia, is the product of a last-minute compromise struck last year at Cop30 in Belém. Australia had wanted to hold a Cop since 2021, when Anthony Albanese made it one of his key promises ahead of the climate-inflected general election he won the next year. Turkey has also wanted to hold a Cop for some time, and claimed to have agreed with the UK, hosts of the Glasgow Cop26 conference in 2021 , that 2026 would be its year.
For complicated reasons dating back to 1992, when the UNFCCC was signed, Australia and Turkey fall in the same group as western Europe when it comes to being allowed to bid for the presidency, which rotates annually between five regional groups. There is no mechanism within the treaty for resolving situations where two countries cannot agree on their bid, and no provision for a majority vote to decide among competing options.
Despite this inauspicious start, the two countries seem to have worked well together in the run-up. Australia will chair the negotiations, taking charge of issues such as the “just transition” to help workers in fossil fuels adjust to a low-carbon economy, the loss and damage fund (which has come into renewed focus after the catastrophic glacier collapse in Nepal ), other forms of climate finance and progress on emissions cuts.
Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, which is a programme of voluntary commitments that runs alongside the formal negotiations. This year, the quest to electrify the global economy will be the central plank, with initiatives on cutting waste and methane – two topics beloved of Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan – also on the list.
Cop31 is also the first major international meeting after several momentous elections: the US midterms, which delivered a pummelling to Donald Trump and the Republicans, and Brazil’s presidential poll, won by the president, Lula da Silva. The latter was regarded as a relief for the Amazon , which Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, was likely to have opened up to further rampant exploitation.
And it is the last such outing for another familiar figure – António Guterres, who has used his two terms as secretary-general of the UN to speak out on the climate as none other . Expect a fiery farewell.
With some items of good news to celebrate, the outlook for Cop31 is not all bleak. But delegates would do well to read the latest UN reports on what it will take to minimise the now inevitable overshoot of the 1.5C threshold. Preventing temperatures rising beyond 1.8C will require massive and urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions, while global carbon emissions have yet to peak. Phasing out fossil fuels has never been so urgent.

Inevitably, the fossil fuel predilections of both hosts will come under scrutiny. Australia could start to shift its reliance on fossil fuel exports in favour of clean electricity, Australia’s Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, told the Guardian when we caught up with him at the mid-year climate talks in Bonn in June. But he refused to put any kind of end date on coal.
Coal remains Turkey’s biggest source of power, despite a push for renewable energy, and the country’s national climate plan allows for an increase in its greenhouse gas emissions, rather than a cut. A group of 50 frontline organisations from Turkey, Australia and other coal regions around the world wrote to the Cop presidents this week to call for an end to coal mining and use.
Mehmet Dalkanat from the Afşin-Elbistan Platform for the Protection of Life and Nature in Turkey said: “People in Afşin-Elbistan have lived with coal for 40 years and have already paid a heavy price in pollution and the impacts of coal.” He points towards the cancellation of plans to expand the country’s largest coal-fired power plant in July. “[This was] a major victory for local communities who have been fighting for years, and a powerful source of hope for a coal-free future,” he said. “The Cop31 presidencies must build on this local victory to accelerate the phaseout of coal and deliver a just transition.”
Though freedom of expression is curtailed in Turkey – as it has been in three of the previous four Cop host countries – expect more such protests in Antalya. We’ll be following developments throughout the summit, with our daily liveblog bringing you news, analysis – and a look behind the scenes of one of the most vital meetings on the planet.

articles.title_orig: Mystery Seller Seeks to Dump $500 Million of Data Center Loans
articles.title_zh: Mystery Seller Seeks to Dump $500 Million of Data Center Loans
articles.content_orig:
ING is reportedly seeking buyers for a portfolio of 12 data center loans worth around $500 million, joining a broader push by banks to distribute credit risk tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out.
The auction is said to include a $25 million piece linked to the Stargate project in New Mexico, which involves OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle , as well as certain other loan assets involving Vantage Data Centers and CyrusOne, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
ING will hold a bids-wanted-in-competition, or BWIC, auction process, with bids sized at $10 million or more due by Nov. 19, according to Bloomberg. A BWIC is a competitive process for investors to bid on pieces of a loan portfolio.
An ING spokesperson declined to comment.
The sale highlights a growing market for banks to move data center loans to private credit firms, asset managers and insurers as financing for the AI boom expands.
Investment banks typically use a lend-to-distribute model for these types of loans, said Hank Calenti, global markets strategist at SMBC.
"The buyers can range from private credit investors through asset managers to insurers. They would buy these assets for their expected higher returns," he said.
The ING sale comes as fears grow over soaring debt tied to the AI build-out — and potentially disappointing returns among investors.
Those concerns have accelerated following the Democrats' sweeping win in the U.S. midterms, which could see moratoriums or tighter restrictions on data center construction in certain states.
The perceived risk of a construction slowdown sent AI-related stocks into free fall on Thursday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closing the session down 5.5% — its worst day since April 2025 — and into correction territory .
"Whether banks sell more based on AI data centers moratorium fears should be driven by the cost (discount received) versus the benefit of exiting to free up cash for further lending, where the cost includes explaining the exposure to your board," Calenti told CNBC via email.
"This could be business as usual, or financiers looking to exit before the door shuts."
Pruksa Iamthongthong, head of APAC equities at Aberdeen Investments, said the Democrats' gains have increased concerns around greater scrutiny of data center development, at a time when investors were already questioning the financing and returns behind the scale of AI capital spending.
"We think near-term volatility could continue as the market assesses potential delays to U.S. data center construction and constraints around compute capacity."
Earlier this year, Wall Street lenders including JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley were said to be exploring a variety of approaches to reduce their lending exposures to data center construction.
According to a Financial Times report on May 3, these include offloading portions of debt via private sales to non-bank lenders, as well as through so-called significant risk transfers, which transfer part of a bank's credit risk to investors to free up balance sheet capacity.

articles.title_orig: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.title_zh: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.content_orig:
Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state"
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title_orig: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.content_orig:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

articles.title_orig: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.title_zh: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.content_orig:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.
Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.
Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.
South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.
Christopher Forbes , head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets , called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining ( via Reuters ):
double quotation mark “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out.
“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.
“And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”
After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.
Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.
Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA , down over 9%.
Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector .
Kyle Rodda , senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.
double quotation mark The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom.
The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.
So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.

3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report
Interestingly, Jefferies economist Mohit Kumar doesn’t believe yesterday’s losses are “the start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
double quotation mark We do admit that policy uncertainty after the Blue Tsunami raises concerns over AI investment and the pace of data center buildup.
However, data centers and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move onto other states or outside the country. AI investment has been a key driver of US growth, and we do not see Democrats as giving up on this growth engine.
There was a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the US stock market yesterday, Jim Reid of Deutche Bank told clients this morning:
double quotation mark In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020 . And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025 .
So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March.
Mohit Kumar, economist at investent bank Jefferies , doesn’t expect a quick rebound from yesterday’s losses.
double quotation mark In previous episodes of retail selling, institutional investors have stepped in to find value. The approaching year-end complicates the behaviour of institutional accounts as risk appetite would be limited….
The geopolitical uncertainty around possible US action in Iran also suggests that investors would not rush to add risk.
Stuart Clark , portfolio manager at Quilter , points out that the dominance of the tech sector exacerbated yesterday’s selloff:
double quotation mark “The blue wave at the ballot box has quickly been replaced by a sea of red on investors’ screens. Technology stocks have sold off sharply, with the immediate catalyst appearing to be concerns around tougher AI regulation, covering both the models themselves and the vast data centre infrastructure required to support them.
“The scale of the falls in some of the market’s biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in US equity markets. With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500.
Ahead of this week’s losses, there were plenty of warning signs that markets might have risen too fast.
As my colleague Richard Partington and I wrote in late September, the warning lights were “flashing red” as the fighting in the Middle East intensified, a slowdown loomed in the AI arms race, and government borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – had risen to its highest level since 2000 by September, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
This week’s losses have pulled the CAPE ratio down ( you can see it here ), but it’s still historically high:
Amid the scary-everything-is-bad-in-stocks news, it’s easy to feel a bit worried about pensions or savings, my colleague Siraj Datoo writes.
And yes, yesterday was a bad day in particular for technology stocks, with the Nasdaq losing $2.5tn in market capital in a single day.
But it’s worth taking a second to pause. While many of the charts leading newspaper homepages are fairly narrow, showing the dramatic fall in just a few days, if you look at the Nasdaq, the US index mostly dominated by tech stocks, from the start of the year, it’s still up 4.6% YTD ( see previous post for more details ).
Of course, this correction still could have room to run and markets are famously emotional. But there have been warnings about this. Michael Burry, the famous fund manager behind The Big Short, has been screaming from the sidelines about overvaluations in the tech world.
One of the major concerns right now is the huge data centre buildout in the US and whether Democrats will place restrictions or slow things down. That’s a problem for investors because so many of the world’s biggest companies have invested enormous amounts of money -- often taking on additional debt -- to fund their deep investment. The bet is that the artificial buildout will eventually generate big returns but investors are now increasingly worried about just how long that will take.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s Congress has refused to accept President Santiago Pena’s resignation, pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings after the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank.
President since 2023, Pena had attempted to resign on Thursday as millions of Ueno customers remained unable to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” the conservative politician said in a recorded address.
But lawmakers declined to accept his resignation. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings, summoning him to appear on Friday.
A joint congressional session called to consider the resignation lost its quorum after lawmakers from Pena’s Colorado Party walked out, as it became clear there were not enough votes to accept it.
Horacio Cartes, a leader in the Colorado Party, had posted a statement on social media indicating the group supported Pena’s impeachment.
“We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds,” Cartes, a former president, wrote in his statement. “We must think of the people and the values we uphold in the Colorado Party.”
Denying Pena’s resignation is likely to heighten the legal jeopardy he faces.
Ordinarily, in Paraguay, presidents who leave office become senators for life, and they enjoy a degree of legal immunity from prosecution as members of the legislature.
But that status is not conferred if the president is convicted in an impeachment trial.
The political crisis erupted earlier this week, when Paraguay’s central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal solvency ratio. Once its books were corrected, the bank’s capital – the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses – was less than half the legal minimum.
Before its collapse, the company claimed it had about 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people. Many have since lost access to their accounts and to pensions paid out through the bank.
As part of a resolution to address the bank’s collapse, Paraguay’s central bank voted to transfer its remaining funds to other financial institutions.
But the central bank itself came under scrutiny for not properly regulating Ueno. The central bank’s head, Carlos Carvallo, has since resigned.
Pena himself formerly held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, though he said he sold those shares in 2025.
Lawmakers, however, have accused Pena of having a conflict of interest and have questioned whether there was an institutional cover-up linked to the lender’s collapse.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“As I speak, there are people outside urging Congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Until its demise, Ueno had grown quickly from a niche company into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850m in public funds.
Paraguay’s attorney general has also ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, which will look into oversight of the lender and the placement of public funds in the institution. Pena has said he will cooperate with investigators.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
If Pena is ultimately removed from office, Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over as president.

articles.title_zh: 12 Planes in 12 Days: Pope Begins Major Latin America Tour, Weeks After Surgery
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.
The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".
It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.
At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".
"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.
"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"
The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.
This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
In all three countries, the Vatican says the Pope will have meetings with survivors of clerical sexual abuse - an issue which clouded a 2018 visit to Chile and Peru by his predecessor.
"This is how the papacy reconnects with Latin America after Francis, whose visits to the region were not always seamless," is how Professor Faggioli sees it.
He believes Pope Leo has a strong sense of the unity of the Americas as one continent. "Democracies are in trouble there, so there are so many things he can address," he suggests.
"The big question then is the United States. There's no question he wants to go. So will he travel when [President Donald] Trump is still in office? I'm sure they're thinking about this."

articles.title_orig: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.title_zh: The IRS has announced new tax brackets for 2027: See where you land
articles.content_orig:
The IRS has announced new federal income tax brackets and standard deductions for 2027.
In its announcement Thursday, the agency raised the income thresholds for each bracket, which apply to tax year 2027 for returns filed in 2028.
The IRS also increased figures for other key provisions, including long-term capital gains brackets, the estate and gift tax exemption , and eligibility for the earned income tax credit, among others.
For 2027, the top rate of 37% applies to individuals with taxable income above $661,375 and married couples filing jointly earning $793,650 or more.
Federal income tax brackets show how much you owe on each part of your taxable income, which you calculate by subtracting the greater of the standard or itemized deductions from your adjusted gross income.
The standard deduction will also increase in 2027, rising to $33,200 for married couples filing jointly, up from $32,200 in 2026. Starting in 2027, single filers can claim $16,600, a bump up from $16,100.
The new tax brackets come as Americans wrestle with affordability issues amid the rising cost of housing , groceries , gasoline and other living expenses.
The consumer price index climbed 3.7% in September 2026 from one year earlier, up from a yearly pace of 3.4% in August, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported in October.
The U.S. federal income tax system is progressive, which means tax rates increase as earnings rise.
For 2027, the federal brackets include seven income tiers, with rates ranging from 10% to 37%. The tax rates apply to each band of income rather than a flat percentage for all earnings.
The IRS adjusts the income ranges for each tax rate yearly based on the consumer price index.
Your federal tax brackets depend on your filing status , which you choose on your tax return. The options include single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household or qualifying surviving spouse.
You can find your 2025 taxable income on line 15 of your individual federal income tax return, known as Form 1040 .

Is the AI bubble bursting?
That question was on the minds of millions of investors on Thursday, as the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) had one of its worst days ever, plunging 5.5% as fears spread that a political backlash could choke the AI boom, following the midterm election.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Investors believe that election winners in Texas and elsewhere will slap significant restrictions or even outright bans on data centers, which became a lightning rod during the campaign. After chip stocks were among the few losers on Wednesday, they collapsed on Thursday, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF losing 11.2%. Even industry leader Nvidia lost 9.1%, and the crash triggered a broader sell-off across the stock market, with all 11 sectors falling, even defensive ones like utilities and consumer staples.
Image source: Getty Images.
AI infrastructure stocks began to wobble a few weeks ago, starting with a chart showing that neocloud operator CoreWeave's (NASDAQ:CRWV) bond yields had risen as high as 15%, and worries about a potential default sent the stock tumbling.
Earnings reports from the big hyperscalers were greeted similarly, as investors worried about soaring capital expenditures and negative free cash flow, even as these companies continue to grow rapidly and are hugely profitable.
Then, the election happened, and now fears of a slowdown in the data center build-out have led investors to flee AI stocks .
Stock market reactions to elections are famously rash and often fleeting. Stocks tumbled following the Brexit decision before bouncing back over the following days, and stocks plunged overnight when President Trump was first elected before turning green the following day.
This looks like a similar reaction. Tech stocks initially fell on Tuesday night before the Nasdaq jumped on Wednesday. The response is understandable as data centers have been a major talking point during the campaign, but the sell-off seems like an overreaction.
Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of Texas, campaigned on a temporary moratorium on data centers and reasonable guidelines, like a ban on subsidies for data centers. However, she is no radical, telling CNN, "We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections."
In a worst-case scenario with a significant slowdown in data center construction in the U.S., most industry observers believe that activity would just move abroad, meaning that industry growth wouldn't be significantly impacted.
In an interview with the Motley Fool, Arm Holdings (NASDAQ:ARM) CFO Jason Child explained his thinking on the matter, saying, "Let's just say it (the data centers) all slows down. Do we believe AI demand will slow down? I think, generally, most people say no. The genie is out of the bottle." Child also said he was generally skeptical of any political reaction and said the bipartisan interest in economic growth was too strong for there to be a significant slowdown in the build-out. He also noted that Arm could still benefit from a slowdown in data center construction, as Arm's chips excel at performance per watt, which would be in greater demand if data center construction were artificially limited.
Predicting where the data center debate goes from here isn't easy, but Child is right that demand for AI is strong and is unlikely to be shaken by any slowdown in capacity growth.
Meanwhile, many of the top AI stocks are looking cheaper than ever. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) now trades at a forward P/E of less than 20, and it's nearly doubling its revenue each quarter. Micron (NASDAQ:MU), the memory chip leader, is trading at a forward P/E of less than 4.
Many of these AI stocks have already soared this year, so the pullback needs to be seen in that context, but like "Liberation Day" and other political issues that have rocked markets, this response seems likely to be an overreaction and a non-issue within the next year. Buying the dip on quality stocks like Nvidia looks like a smart move.

The steep sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks likely has further to go, CNBC's Jim Cramer predicted Thursday — but he urged investors not to panic.
Growing opposition to new data centers following the midterm elections has raised doubts about future AI infrastructure spending, sending shares of companies tied to the buildout sharply lower. Micron tumbled 17%, GE Vernova dropped 7% and Sandisk plunged 22% on Thursday. All three stocks were also crushed in Wednesday's session.
"I wish I could say that today's flush was the bottom," the " Mad Money " host said, before cautioning that there may be more downside ahead, though he didn't believe this was an internet bubble redux. Cramer argued that today's AI companies are fundamentally different from the speculative businesses that collapsed during the dot-com bust.
"But I look at the charts, and there still seems like there's no support for so many Tech stocks, especially the semis, because they ran so much on the way up. However it might feel, it's actually an orderly decline because unlike 2000, these are mostly lucrative companies with stocks that went too high."
Investors had pushed AI stocks too high by assuming the rapid pace of data center construction would continue indefinitely, Cramer said. Smaller developers such as CoreWeave , Iren and Nebius face particular risks because they borrowed money to finance projects that could now face regulatory delays.
"That's what I am chiefly worried about," he said. "That's the real problem. That's what could really hurt the stock market. ... Right now, no one of significance is defaulting on their debt. The only issue with the debt is that it's connected to those neocloud companies that I mentioned. That's not enough to sink us."
Cramer suggested that a swift sell-off could help the market work off the excesses of the AI boom more effectively than a prolonged downturn.
"I for one am glad they are ripping the Band-Aid off this market rather than slowing trying to take it off a little bit each day," he said.
For investors, Cramer recommended maintaining sufficient cash. While semiconductor stocks could face further declines, he pointed to falling interest rates, signs of easing inflation and the possibility of an end to the Iran war as reasons for optimism.
"If you have cash you won't panic," Cramer concluded. "You won't be complacent, either. You will be clear-headed and that's how you will lose less money until things get better. They always do."
